title: Styles and Adaptability
description: Negotiators tend toward competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, or accommodating. The most effective negotiators adapt their style to the situation and counterpart.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Negotiators tend toward competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, or accommodating. The most effective negotiators adapt their style to the situation and counterpart.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A competitor opens with a strong anchor and gives little. Useful for a one-time car purchase, destructive for a long-term partnership.
A collaborator asks many questions, explores interests, and builds creative packages. High-value in joint ventures, slow and exposed with a purely distributive counterpart.
An avoider postpones tough issues, hoping they'll go away. Works only for trivial matters.

sections.title: Practical Adaptation Strategy
content: If the other side opens aggressively and you don't need a relationship, compete back.
If you need ongoing cooperation, shift to collaborative by asking, 'How can we structure this so we both get what's most important?'
If the other side avoids, gently surface the issue: 'I notice we haven't talked about budget yet. I'd like to address it today so we don't hit a problem later.'

sections.title: Common Mistake
sections.content: Using the same style for every negotiation. Purely collaborative with a shark gets you eaten; purely competitive with a partner kills trust.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Style is a tool, not an identity. Pick the tool that fits the job.
